Wait, so you mean that the value of shares is based largely on perception, and not on any physical quantity? If that is the case then why does it matter if a company's share is overvalued?

I agree, The explanation needs to be correct though. :)

tldr; There are two main things; profit and the number of shares. Companies have a certain number of shares, as they make a profit the number of shares don't change so each one becomes more valuable.

shares represent ownership of a company. When a company "goes public" it essentially means it's stable enough for the general public to own a chunk of. Companies make money (the fancy word is earnings.). When companies are profitable they make more money which means (with the shares staying the same) each share gains value. People try to guess if a company will make a profit and how much, also if the amount of profit is growing. These guesses (fancy word: estimates) can impact the price which is why the stock price doesn't always align with the "profit divided over the number of shares ratio"

The value of a company is simply the value of a share multiplied by total number of shares.

If a company is doing well it may take some (or all) of its profit and give it out to the shareholders (this is called dividends).

Also, if a company is doing well more people will want to buy its shares, which increases demand, and increases the price of the shares.

Ok, let's try ELI5-ing this (I'm an active trader).

Shares are valued based on supply/demand as you said. The price goes up if people buy more shares, and down if people sell more shares.

People buy shares if they think the price will go up & sell if they think it will go down. Which directly makes the price go up and down.

Dividends are paid on a schedule directly from the company's profits on a per share basis. Say, $0.05 per share, and you own 1000 shares, you get $50.00 basically for free, from their profits, every month (as an example). The $/share changes based on the companies profits.

TL;DR: Shares get their value based on how much money is directly invested in the company which is based on how much the market says the company is worth. It's basically that simple.
